baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Sugar’s changing uses connect consumption to colonial production and industrial work
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Mintz’s “Sugar,” opening paragraphs1–8, explains the historical route from Caribbean fieldwork through a commodity’s global markets and human costs. His primary retrospective supports this scoped contribution; complete Sweetness and Power remains unread.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: A cane worker’s narrated life becomes a perspective on Puerto Rican labour history
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: In the Thomas interview, sectionIV, Mintz explains returning to work with Taso and constructing a personal account alongside Puerto Rican history. The worker’s interpretation is part of the inquiry. Mintz’s claim to absolute disciplinary priority is not adopted.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: With Richard Price, cultural formation is studied through new circumstances and social institutions
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Baud(2011),263, explicitly identifies this joint1976/1992 inquiry. This named reader supports the scoped connection; it does not imply identical Afro-American cultures or prove influence on all Atlantic historians. Joint authorship and distinct editions are retained; primary essay unread.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Plantation provisioning and peasant activity expose tensions within colonial economic organization
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Baud(2011),260, reads Caribbean Transformations as explaining provision grounds and emerging peasant practices within plantation society. This is Baud’s specific account of Mintz’s contribution, not a catalogue-derived argument or a general claim that all customary markets shared one logic.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Greene credits cooperation with Mintz and Richard Price in sustaining the interdisciplinary Atlantic History and Culture program he helped organize at Johns Hopkins.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own retrospective answer identifies actual Anthropology Department cooperation over several decades and describes the original interdisciplinary program rather than mere shared employment. Richard Price retains joint credit; his endpoint is absent. This is a bounded collaborative intellectual setting, not proof of Mintz’s sole authorship, a specific book debt or personal formation. Precise institutional chronology not independently audited. Philip D.Morgan is a distinct absent-endpoint successor/coeditor, not Edmund S.Morgan.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Mintz connects changing sugar consumption with colonial slave production, industrial labor and capitalism
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. Publisher description now checked for this specific argument; the full book and reception remain unreviewed.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Mintz and Price connect cultural continuity to forced-migration conditions
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: The HLAS scholarly annotation identifies their 1976 methodological argument. This contribution is not proof of influence on every Atlantic historian; the primary essay and its critics remain to be read.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Named ethnographic studies inform Thompson’s questions about time and markets
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Time essay pp. 58–59 uses Evans-Pritchard and Bourdieu; Moral Economy p. 135 invokes Mintz on markets. These are distinct resources, not a uniform anthropological model or proof that his cultural comparisons generalize universally.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Van Gennep’s folklore and Douglas on pollution and boundaries, then Evans-Pritchard, Turner, Geertz and Mintz, read for questions tested on sixteenth-century evidence (1969–1980s)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Her acknowledgements, in period and in retrospect. 1973 (read): ‘For the theory in this paragraph, I have found helpful Mary Douglas’s remarks on the relation between pollution fears and concern for social boundaries (Purity and Danger … ch. 7)’ (p. 61, n. 25); Van Gennep’s Manuel de folklore français on the dead (p. 57, n. 17). 1997 (read in full): she found Van Gennep’s Manuel, but her essay ‘used only historical evidence’ and, ‘in contrast with the static unchanging portrait of ceremonial and customary life presented in Van Gennep’, ‘pointed to shifts’ (p. 14); ‘I went on to read in anthropology and folklore: E.E. Evans-Pritchard, Victor Turner, Clifford Geertz, Sidney Mintz, and many others … I read eclectically, indifferent to conflicts within anthropology, for I was not looking for solutions, but for questions’ (p. 14); ‘One term I co-taught a course with Clifford Geertz’ (p. 19); the Martin Guerre project ‘grew out of the practice of anthropological history’ (p. 17). Finlay (1988, p. 554, read) attributes the book’s ‘inventive aspects’ to ‘anthropology, ethnography, and literary criticism’. No single anthropologist is credited as the source, and no specifically Geertzian method is established.
